@Heckerman_1995 address learning Bayesian networks from a combination of

The Bayesian information criterion goes back to @Schwarz_1978.

## Sample size

<!-- Search of 26 November 2026: web search, arXiv, Crossref and DataCite. Not
     systematic. Zuk et al. read in full; the others from their abstracts, except
     Constantin et al., cited for what its title states. Not cited because it
     could not be matched to a record: Dai, Korb, Wallace and Wu (1997), IJCAI,
     on weak links and small samples, which Zuk et al. cite. Read it before
     submitting. -->

A penalized score tends to miss real arrows in small samples. @Zuk_2006 study how
many samples are needed to learn the correct structure of a Bayesian network of
binary variables with the BIC. They separate two errors. One is preferring a
structure that cannot represent the true distribution, for example one that lacks
a real arrow. The other is preferring a structure with more parameters than
needed. The first error falls exponentially with sample size and the second falls
as a power of it, so the second dominates in large samples. In small samples the
first is the more likely error. In their example with four variables, it was the
more likely error below 2,000 samples.

Learning the correct structure also needs more data than approximating the
distribution [@Zuk_2006], a task whose sample complexity @Friedman_1996 analyze.
@Koivisto_2006 studies by simulation the statistical power of a Bayesian method
of structure learning, with 20 to 10,000 records and 5 to 25 variables. In their
own simulations, @Scutari_2013 report that the sensitivity of their rule for
keeping arrows rises linearly with the logarithm of sample size. Bootstrap resampling
gives a measure of confidence in each arrow [@Friedman_1999]. For another family
of network models, @Constantin_2026 propose a Monte Carlo method of sample size
analysis.

## Other ways to test a diagram

A diagram implies independencies that can be checked in data, for example with
the `dagitty` package [@Ankan_2021]. @Eulig_2023 compare the number of such
violations with the number found after shuffling the variables among the boxes.
@Pitchforth_2013 propose a validation framework for expert-elicited Bayesian
networks.

## Applications to farm and food decisions

<!-- Question: where have expert causal diagrams informed agricultural
     decisions, and were they tested? -->

One example from our group concerns decision tools for agricultural development
policy and household nutrition [@Whitney_2018].

## Gap

<!-- Question: what do the sections above leave open that hcbic addresses? -->

<!-- NOVELTY: that small samples make BIC reject real arrows is NOT new
     (Zuk et al. 2006). Do not present it as a finding of this work. -->

The finding that small samples lead the BIC to reject real arrows agrees with
@Zuk_2006. `hcbic` applies the idea to one expert-elicited diagram of
agroforestry. It reports the sample size needed arrow by arrow, under the
expert's own probabilities, and shows which arrows those probabilities make
undetectable.

The structure learning in `hcbic` uses the `bnlearn` package [@Scutari_2010].
